learning_objective: 🎯 [Students will apply advanced determiners to specify nouns accurately and use modal auxiliaries to express nuance in attitude, obligation, possibility, and permission.]
warm_up_hook: 🎛️ Determiners are the bouncers deciding who gets into the noun club, while Modals are the mood-rings of verbs, showing exactly how likely, necessary, or polite an action is! Time to fine-tune your sentences! 🎚️

lesson_modules.teaching_content: Beyond basic articles, 11th-grade grammar requires precision with quantifiers (few vs. a few, little vs. a little). 'Few/Little' means almost none (negative tone), while 'a few/a little' means some (positive tone). We also learn when NOT to use articles (Zero Article) for abstract nouns or general plural concepts.
examples_or_templates: A few vs Few: I have a few friends (positive, some). I have few friends (negative, almost none).
Zero Article: Life is beautiful. (General abstract concept, no 'the')

lesson_modules.module_title: 🔮 Modals of Certainty, Probability, and Ability
lesson_modules.teaching_content: Modals do not change form with subjects. For ability, we use Can/Could. For deduction/certainty, we use Must (strong positive deduction), Can't (strong negative deduction), and May/Might/Could (possibility).
examples_or_templates: Strong Deduction: He has been working for 12 hours. He MUST be exhausted.
Possibility: Take an umbrella; it MIGHT rain later.

lesson_modules.module_title: ⚖️ Modals of Obligation, Advice, and Permission
lesson_modules.teaching_content: To express duty or necessity, we use Must or Have to (Must is internal obligation, Have to is external rule). For advice, we use Should or Ought to. For permission, May is formal, while Can is informal.
examples_or_templates: Obligation: You HAVE TO wear a uniform at this school. (External rule)
Advice: You OUGHT TO apologize for your mistake.

practice_mcq_quiz.question: ❓ Choose the correct option: 'I have _____ patience left for this ridiculous argument.'
❓ Which modal best completes the deduction? 'You just ate a huge meal. You _____ be hungry again already!'

subjective_practice.question: ✍️ Fill in the blanks with 'much' or 'many': 'We don't have _____ time before the train arrives, so don't bring _____ bags.'
subjective_practice.hint: Use 'much' for uncountable nouns (time) and 'many' for countable nouns (bags).

subjective_practice.question: ✍️ Rewrite this sentence using a suitable modal: 'It is strictly prohibited to park your car in front of the hospital.'
subjective_practice.hint: Use a modal that shows strict negative obligation (e.g., must not).

subjective_practice.question: ✍️ Fill in the blank with the correct modal (should, would, could, might): 'If I had studied harder, I _____ have passed the exam.'
subjective_practice.hint: This is a past conditional sentence referring to a past ability or possibility.

activity_or_assignment.title: 📜 The School Rulebook
activity_or_assignment.instructions: Draft a mini-rulebook for a fictional, ultra-strict magical academy. Write 3 rules using determiners correctly (e.g., 'Every student...') and 3 rules using modals of obligation/prohibition (e.g., 'Students must not...').

chapter_summary: ⭐ 'Few/Little' indicate a negative lack of something, whereas 'A few/A little' indicate a positive presence of some amount.
⭐ Modals express the speaker's attitude regarding possibility (might/may), ability (can/could), and logical deduction (must/can't).
⭐ Modals of obligation distinguish between internal duty (must), external rules (have to), and advice (should/ought to).
